paragraphs.text: Welcome back to another episode of Tis the Podcast, the podcast that's determined to keep the Christmas spirit alive 366 days per year. I'm Anthony.
I'm Julia.
I'm Thom.
I'm Todd.
Todd! Welcome back, Todd.
Hey, guys. Thanks for having me again.
We're so glad you could come down from the North Pole to be on a podcast episode with us. How's your brother Santa doing?
He's well. He's napping, as one should do in the off-season.
Yes, as one should do when you have an army of slaves to make all your gifts for you.
Yeah, he's in the self-quarantine right now.
Oh, what a great place to quarantine. The North Pole.
I mean, isn't their whole 364 days a year just quarantine anyway?

Right. I mean, if you're on the floor of that workshop, they're always all together, so they'd have to quarantine together. They just quarantine as a unit, you know? The North Pole is quarantined together, and their elf biology protects them from COVID.
Yeah, you've got to keep all the Etch A Sketch elves away from all the jack-in-the-box elves.
Sure. They might need to do a little separation.
So, y'all will recognize Todd's dulcet tones from the Christmas Clatter podcast. But also, wait, you have a podcast, Todd?
Yep.
This is news! Can you tell everybody about this Christmas Clatter Anthony speaks of?

Well, Christmas Clatter is the podcast that celebrates everything that makes Christmas special. We just turned one year old last month, in May, and we have episodes that come out on the 15th and 30th of each month. And I think if all goes according to schedule, my next Christmas conversation, for the 30th of June, should be some terrible guy named Thom Crowe.
Come on!
In June. He is super excited.
Don't forget, you promised to ask both of them as well about the origins of our show, to see how they overlap or not.
Yep, yep. And then last time I talked with Julia, she was planning on coming on in October. I wanted to spread you guys out a little bit.
Yes. And, yeah, special. She gets closer to the Christmas season than any of us.
I'm spread out as far as I can be.
I was telling Anthony earlier, I said it's almost a year to the date from when I made my Tis the Podcast debut last year with The 12 Dates of Christmas.
Oh, that's right.
So now I've taken up a permanent June residency on Tis the Podcast.
I think that's great. June is Todd month. We've got to go back to themed months, and then when people ask, "What's June?" Todd Killian.

And also, listeners, you heard me and Julia joking earlier about Todd being Santa's brother. We'll plug it again toward the end of the episode when we talk about Patreon, but listen to Todd's fireside chat, because it is the most magical conversation you will ever hear with somebody who is not Santa Claus himself.
True. Allegedly.
Allegedly not Santa Claus. Have any of us seen Todd in the month of December?
No.
I get a little bit more gray in my beard each and every day, so you just never know.
Pulling a Scott Calvin from the months.
It's that or the four kids. I'm not sure which one it is. Oh, I think it's the four kids.
Your kids must be real good. Have you seen my beard and I only have one?
I have to plug a product here.
I try not to drink soda, but then I found this. Dr. Pepper with cream soda? It tastes like Christmas soda.
Christmas soda. It does. Christmas soda? I want one. It does. I'm unfortunately drinking soda because my espresso machine came in early and I don't have espresso beans to grind.
I'm so sorry, Thom. Do you drink those espressos with your pinky out?
What do you think? He has those espresso cups that don't have a handle, that you just grip.
I know. Do you just hold them like that?
Right. Oh my gosh, I was right.
Well, you have to use those double-walled glass things, otherwise it gets too hot.
Oh, Thom, I love your coffee ways.
I do want to plug a product, too. I want to plug this new microphone I got.
You sound delightful.
Thank you, Julia. That's the first time anybody's ever said that about me in my life.
I think it's true every single week.
Oh, that might be the nicest thing you've ever said to me on the show. It's going to get… don't worry. This whole show is about being nice to Anthony.
That's debatable.
No, this episode. Not the whole podcast, just today.
Okay. We're almost halfway to Christmas. I'm feeling the Christmas spirit.
We are almost halfway to Christmas. You do sound really good. And that's a mighty good-looking microphone as well. Where'd you get it?
Amazon.
Oh, there might be one in the mail on the way to you right now, Julia.
Oh, I will. Hopefully it'll be here before next week. Christmas in June!
Now, listeners, don't take that to mean Thom is a very generous guy. Julia, he did not pay for it for Julia. He just ordered it and had it shipped. I want to clear up that misconception.
So far there's not been any reimbursement yet, so so far it's just a gift.
We'll rectify that before the wife looks at the credit card.
Excuse me, sending fancy gifts to other women? Who are you buying microphones for?
It was Anthony, I swear.
No, I bought it myself, Thom. Don't use me as an excuse.
So, Todd, what brings you to the show tonight?

Lethal Weapon. You guys had mentioned covering Lethal Weapon, since it has Christmas in it, and this is a movie that has been dear to my childhood since the mid-'80s. And I got on Messenger like, "If you guys do Lethal Weapon, please, please, please, can I come on?"
Well, I feel bad for making you wait, because I remember when we initially recorded that fireside chat with you, we thought it was scheduled for like the next week, and here we are.
Oh, it's fine if it's four months later. I'm used to it. I know how you guys operate.
We did do better this time. We didn't have a million reschedulings like we did last June.
Oh, we did. I'm so sorry. That was bad. Do you remember that?
I had a bad couple of days, but I'm still here for you, Todd.
Wait, Todd must be bad luck for you, Thom. Remember last year? We didn't hear from you. You were asleep, so me and Julia canceled, and you were pissed off at us. That was the Todd episode.
He was overseas, in London or something.
It was the situation. You were a little annoyed.
You were super annoyed.
I was cranky. My sleep was off. I apologize. There's no excuse for treating anybody in a way that's frustrated, and I apologized.
You did.

I have a little thing about this movie. I wasn't allowed to watch this movie as a kid, and I hear Todd was. Were there any movies you remember not being allowed to watch as a kid? And I'm going to go on while you're thinking of that. The one for me is Pretty Woman. I still have not watched that movie, because my grandparents were so against me seeing it that I still have this fear of watching it.
If you watched Lethal Weapon last week, then Pretty Woman's a walk in the park.

There wasn't as much, none of that, because they said, oh, for whatever reason, my family was very opposed to me watching Pretty Woman. For Christine as a kid, we were talking about this, she was not allowed to watch The Bodyguard and still never watched it for the same reason. Oh, interesting.
Wake up, Ellie!

Oh my gosh. There was never a movie I couldn't watch as a kid. My parents gauged what movies me and my sister could watch by whether we were mentally capable of handling it, whether it was violence or whatever. They were wary of horror films, but that's because I was easily scared as a child. But I saw Scream when I was in sixth grade. They said, "If you want to watch it, you can watch it." I got through that opening scene with Drew Barrymore and was like, "I'm out," and then I finished it the next year.

Yeah, I remember watching, I forget which Nightmare on Elm Street it was, the one with Johnny Depp and the waterbed, when I was a kid. I was going to bed for like a month just lying there on my bed, wide-eyed.
But you know that scene was an accident, right, Thom? The room spun out of control, and that's how the blood came spurting out.
Oh, really? It wasn't supposed to?
The set was rotating, and they lost control of it, and all the blood came out that way. And they liked it so much they used the shot.
Like one of those Spirograph thingies that I used to play with all the time.
Like the scene in Inception.

That's funny. I was never allowed to watch any horror movies. I was not allowed to watch The X-Files, ever. I snuck episodes in high school and then watched the rest of them in college, because my mom thought it was satanic.
There's a lot I was not allowed to watch. Movies like this, I could watch if they were on TV, edited for TV, which I feel like used to happen pretty regularly back then.
Right. I think it still does, on FX and channels like that.

But Todd, you mentioned Nightmare on Elm Street. The first R-rated movie I ever saw in theaters, to show you guys how young I am, was Freddy vs. Jason, which is basically their last movie before the reboots.
Oh, wow. I forget I'm the old guy with you guys around.
I'm up there with you.
I think all three of us, except for Anthony, are on the same plane for the most part. But no, I was able to watch this movie when I was a kid, and I just had to hide my eyes in certain parts.

Well, I think that's a good segue. Maybe we should do a little disclaimer that there are definitely adult themes in this movie that we'll probably touch upon, so you might want to listen when small children aren't around. And there's your warning.
So, Lethal Weapon. Julia, do you want to give us a plot synopsis?

Martin Riggs is an LA cop with suicidal tendencies, and Roger Murtaugh is the unlikely police officer with whom Riggs is assigned. Together they uncover a huge drug-smuggling operation, and as their success rate grows, so does their friendship.
Oh, that's a good one. That's a good one.

Oh, dear. So this movie was directed by Richard Donner, who's probably most known for Superman: The Movie and the Superman II director's cut, which came out years later. But he also directed movies like The Goonies and Scrooged. This is not the first time that we've covered Richard Donner, so I'll leave it at that.

And also not the first time we're covering the writer. Shane Black wrote this movie. We covered him with Iron Man 3, we're going to cover him later this year with Kiss Kiss Bang Bang, and he also did classics such as The Monster Squad, which I love, The Last Boy Scout, Last Action Hero, The Long Kiss Goodnight, The Nice Guys, and The Predator.
This movie stars what would go on to become an iconic cinematic pairing after this film: Mel Gibson as Martin Riggs, before Mel Gibson went off the rails in his later life.
Is this the first time we… I feel like Mel…
No, it's not the first time we've covered him.
Speaking of going off the rails, there must be something in the water of this film, because it also has Gary Busey.
Oh, man. A little off the rails there as well.

Yeah. Well, we'll get to Gary Busey in a minute, because I have something to say about Gary Busey. Now, Gibson does have another Christmas connection coming up. I mentioned this during the Daddy's Home 2 episode, at which point he had just signed on, I believe, but he is attached to play Santa Claus in the independent action comedy movie Fatman.
I wonder if he's going to be a traditional Santa or more of a Kurt Russell Santa.
I can't tell if that's sarcasm.
No, I don't know. I haven't seen any pictures. I don't know what it's going to be like.
I haven't either. But from what I know of Mel Gibson, he's not going to sign on to play Mr.
Cuddly, fat guy.

He might be trying to clean up his image, though. Speaking of... Okay, I'm derailing. I'm sorry. Speaking of Kurt Russell as Santa, is that the first thing you saw when you saw that new awesome rad Christmas Santa sticker? Yes! I told Jerry that when he showed it to me. I loved it. I'm like, man, that is... That is... growing on me as my Santa, maybe, after Ed Asner didn't even phone it in on our shout-out from Cameo. He's old. Cut that out, Julia, because people loved that Cameo. People did love that. It was such crap. It still gave me a thrill to hear him mention the podcast and our names. It did. I guess you could call them elves. That was a waste of $200.

That was the part that makes Sarah laugh the most when he was like, we'll pretend they're the elves. He doesn't know Danny. It went over his head. I don't think it has anything to do with him being old. I think he was drunk off of his gourd.
Danny Glover. Well, that would have been... Drunk off of his gourd would have been a good one. Segway for Mel Gibson. Mel Gibson.

Playing Mel Gibson's partner, playing Mel Gibson's partner, Roger Murtaugh, is Danny Glover. who has had an amazing career. He's probably best known for the Lethal Weapon film series, but he was also in The Color Purple, Predator 2, Angels in the Outfield. The Christmas Train.

Oh, we've covered him before too. So I don't even have to go through all of his credits. Now, when I say I'm being nice to Anthony, did you see I didn't stop you and correct you? I just threw in a bit of, I just threw in a crumb for you to pick up and run with.
Also, he...
So, Danny Glover. I always mix him up with Donald Glover, the first name.
Me too!
He is not Childish Gambino.

No, he is not. But I remember after I saw Spider-Man: Homecoming, which Donald Glover was in. He was the crook who Tom Holland webs to the car to interrogate, and he had the name of Miles Morales's uncle, who goes on to become a supervillain later on. Anyway, when I talked to my friend, I was like, "Oh yeah, and Danny Glover played Miles Morales's uncle. He's going to be a villain later on." And they're like, "Danny Glover?" I was like, "Yeah, Danny Glover." They're like, "You mean Donald Glover?" Yes. And then I did the opposite when I was talking about Solo. I was like, "Oh man, Danny Glover's playing Lando Calrissian."
Oh, that's funny. Danny Glover's also in Shooter with Mark Wahlberg, and for some reason he whispers through the whole movie. It's like, what is he saying?
Danny Glover also made me super uncomfortable within the first five minutes of this film.
Yes, but we'll talk about that in a few minutes. Correct me if I'm wrong, but the only other person I really want to mention is Gary Busey. Everyone else is just kind of…
No, no, no, no. You've got to mention
Darlene Love. Yeah, you've got to mention Darlene Love. Darlene Love plays Are we going to not talk Gary Busey? We're saving the best for last.
I'm so excited to talk about Nick Nolte's look-alike.
Darlene Love plays Trish Murtaugh, Danny Glover's wife.
And she performed on the celebrated Christmas album A Christmas Gift for You from Phil Spector in 1963.

Yes. She won an Oscar for 20 Feet from Stardom, a documentary on background singers, in 2014 or '16, I can't remember which. It's on Netflix, and for anybody that hasn't seen it, go watch it. It is excellent.
So good.

Yes. She tells a story in there. She's the original lady that recorded "Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)" for that 1963 album. And Phil Spector really did her dirty through her musical career in the '60s. She would record stuff, and then he would say it was the Ronettes or some other group, the Crystals, that did it, when it was her. So she was missing out on this money, so she quit. She just walked out on him after all these years of singing, and she was cleaning houses to make a living. And then her version of "Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)" comes on the radio, because it's close to Christmastime, and she's like, "That's me. What am I doing cleaning houses?" And so, midlife, she decides to pick up her career again, and it takes off. She lands this acting role and some other roles and starts singing and things again. It's a really incredible story, and it's in that documentary along with other ladies that stood behind bands like the Rolling Stones and things like that, that you wouldn't have any idea how awesome they are, and they never got credit. So definitely check out 20 Feet from Stardom. It's worth a watch for sure.
Now, Todd, I don't ever want to call bull on a guest host, but do you really expect me to believe that Phil Spector treated somebody with anything other than respect?
Yeah, I mean, as you're telling this, I'm like, of course he did.
Yeah. He was a tortured genius, but man. I don't know how those people survived all of it.

Well, I am glad that she found her place back in. Speaking of tortured geniuses: Gary Busey, aka the man I always thought missed his calling playing the Joker when he was younger, plays our villain in this piece, Mr. Joshua. Where to start with Gary Busey?
You talked about how you got Donald and Danny Glover mixed up. I always got Gary Busey and Nick Nolte mixed up, all the time.
That has to make you feel really sad for Nick Nolte.
Yeah, it does. Little trivia for you: Gary Busey has Tulsa, Oklahoma, roots. He was born in Texas and grew up in Oklahoma. So, America, on behalf of the state of Oklahoma, you're welcome.
You're welcome, brother.
Seriously, I feel bad for this guy. Watching his life, it's like watching a whole train wreck happening right in front of you.

Well, he's most famous, or at least he's got the most acclaim, for playing Buddy Holly in The Buddy Holly Story, for which he was nominated for an Academy Award. He was in Predator 2, Point Break, Under Siege, The Firm, Carried Away, Black Sheep, Lost Highway, Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, The Gingerdead Man, Quigley, and Piranha 3DD. He's also had guest appearances on such shows as Gunsmoke, Walker, Texas Ranger, Law & Order, Scrubs, Impractical Jokers, and Entourage.
So I feel like you're missing some pretty important things here.
He was in the TV show From Dusk Till Dawn.
I don't know if y'all saw that. It was terrible.
There's a TV show?

He was on the WWE Legends' House on the WWE Network. He was in Sharknado 4 and the fifth Sharknado, The Last Sharknado: It's About Time. He also played himself in Celebrity Paranormal Project, where four out of five celebrity participants are taken to an allegedly haunted location during the night and left until sunrise, with the task of identifying paranormal activity.
Oh my gosh. Wait, hold on, we've got to see who was in his episode.
Jenna Maraska, Takara Jones, Donna D'Errico, and Hal Sparks.
Wasn't he on The Apprentice or something?
They are all B- and C-list celebrities, so probably. And then, what is your favorite Gary Busey movie? Not necessarily role, because there's a big difference.
Sharknado 5: The Last One, It's About Time. That's a good one.
I'm joking. I mean, I do love Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas.
Nobody's given the right answer yet. Julia, do you want to try to get the right answer?
Was he the one in that kids' baseball movie? Or was that the other one, where he had to ice his arm all the time and he blew his arm out? It was one of those Disney movies.
Angels in the Outfield? That was Tony Danza, right?
That was Tony Danza. Okay, so then
Rookie of the Year. Was he in Rookie of the Year, or was that Nick Nolte?
I'm assuming if he was around children, it would be Nick Nolte.
No, you're wrong.
I'm wrong. It was him. That's probably my favorite one. I loved that movie when I was a kid. My favorite baseball movie is The Sandlot. I love that movie.
I never asked your favorite baseball movie. I asked your favorite Gary Busey movie.
No, I know, but you just mentioned Angels in the Outfield, and I wanted to get that in there.
I love The Sandlot. So many boys. Wendy Peppercorn, my heart.
The correct answer is Point Break.
Point Break's your favorite?
As the best movie that Nick Nolte was in, yes.
I was never allowed to see that movie.
You should.
Says the guy who still hasn't watched Pretty Woman. Todd, what did you say yours was?
I like The Buddy Holly Story quite a bit, but probably the one I've seen the most out of all those is Under Siege.

Are you a Steven Seagal fan? He's so bad in that one too. At the time, you know, at that window of time in the early mid-90s. Every boy was a Steven Seagal fan back then. Oh, he was a role with Dolly Parton. Oh, Bolero.
Dolly Parton.

So Lethal Weapon, like its spiritual successor a year and a half later, Die Hard, is one of those films that constantly appears on lists around Christmastime, with Batman Returns and Gremlins and a few of these other movies you've talked about, on these lists of non-Christmas Christmas movies that are perfect for people who want to celebrate the holiday without getting into those overly sentimental classics that we all love. So I'm curious to see where we all fall on that question, whether it's a Christmas movie or just a movie set at Christmas. I'm sure that'll come up in our histories a bit and then get fleshed out during discussion. So let's dive into histories. Guests first. Todd?

I guess I saw this movie… it was released in '87? Okay. So I probably saw this movie, I didn't see it in theaters. Back then it usually took about a year before they came out on video, so I imagine we went and rented it and watched it. And at the time it was one of the first, if not the first, pure action movie that had some comedy in it, where you could laugh. I remember it being so different than anything we'd seen before, and I've just loved it ever since. And when I rewatched it, it wasn't as funny as I remember, because I think the series gets funnier as it goes, through two, three, and four. And just a bit of trivia there: Shane Black left the franchise as writer because of how funny they were making it. They kept taking out more and more action and supplementing it with more and more jokes.
Right. This is definitely the darkest of the four.

This is definitely the darkest of the four. But I just remember renting it when I was a kid and watching it with my dad and cracking up, and just thinking how great it was, as far as being something different from what we'd seen before. Of course, the action comedy isn't anything new anymore, but in my opinion, this is kind of where it started. I think that's where that genre got popular, and where the whole buddy-cop thing got popular.
Right. Where do you fall on the Christmas question?

Well, I'm a notoriously easy grader as far as Christmas movies. As long as there's Christmas in it, I usually give it a pass. And I mean, this movie starts off with Bobby Helms' "Jingle Bell Rock," and there are Christmassy scenes set up in it. The story doesn't revolve around Christmas, but I'll give it a pass and call it a Christmas movie.

So I'll just piggyback off that with my history. I saw this when I was a child, sometime after Die Hard. Again, they're very similar movies in a lot of ways. Mel Gibson even went out for the Die Hard part, and Bruce Willis went for the Lethal Weapon part. And I much prefer Die Hard, for a few reasons. Number one, while it's an '80s movie, it's an '80s movie that does not feel anywhere near as dated as this movie does. That was the primary thought I had while watching this film this morning for the show: how dated this felt, from the music to the styles to that cheesy '80s saxophone interlude in between scenes. So I think when you compare the two, Die Hard holds up.
Yeah, I think some of that's because Die Hard takes place in one building the whole time.
Right. And this goes through the rainiest Los Angeles anybody has ever seen. Has anybody ever been to LA? I ain't seen rain like that, ever.

I mean, if it's Chicago or New York, I've seen rain like that there. I have never been in LA during rain. And that goes on to my next point: this is not a Christmas movie for me. Not at all. Not in the slightest, compared to Die Hard.
That is a gauntlet thrown down, dude.

This is not a Christmas movie. It's a movie set at Christmas. Christmas had nothing to do with the plot. At least Die Hard took place at the Christmas party, the Christmas Eve work party. All that to say, I like this movie. I still like it. It's fun, just not as good to me as Die Hard, which is the closest thing we have to compare it to on our list. So, Julia, how about you?

So I first saw this movie when I was probably a teenager. I don't know how much of a teenager, but again, it would have had to come out on TV in an edited form for me to see it. So pick your teenage year. My brother and I love movies like this, and my dad loves movies like this. So it probably came on, and my dad had probably seen it, and it was like, "Hey, we need to watch this." So we watched it as a family, as a lot of my '80s action movies were unveiled to me, in the exact same fashion.
Right.
And I have always loved Mel Gibson. He's a big part of my childhood. So many good movies I can name off that I love Mel
Gibson in, and we kind of loved him as a family.
Because this is an audio medium, just so our listeners know, Mel Gibson is staring at Julia this evening.
He is. His eyes. He's super handsome, Mel Gibson, too, because the younger Mel Gibson was just really quite cute.
So you're into men with big feathery hair?
I was when this one came out, for sure.

I also like Die Hard more than this movie, but I saw Die Hard more than this movie. I think my dad probably liked Die Hard more, my brother liked Die Hard more, and so by virtue, I liked Die Hard more. I really loved watching this again, though. I watched it yesterday, because I hadn't seen it in a really long time, and I had never seen the unedited, not-for-TV version, so it did fill some gaps in. When I think back now, I'm like, I don't even know what they're talking about half the time. But I'm in this movie for the action. It is a movie set at Christmas. It's not a Christmas movie. And I could almost chalk it up more to nostalgia, why I think Die Hard is a Christmas movie and why I think this is not, because it's a very fine line between the two, honestly.

And I think people that don't have nostalgia built up for either one would say, you can't call Die Hard a Christmas movie and not call this one a Christmas movie. I would argue that, but I'm sure we'll get into that in more detail later on. It is interesting to me though, right off the bat that both of them are set in LA as opposed to Chicago and New York, like the traditional Christmas movies. That feel more Christmassy. So I love this movie. What's that? Anthony, when you say that you would like to discuss that, I very much look forward to hearing your valid arguments on why this is not a Christmas movie.
He's got a full NPR voice.
Yes, I am here to bring to you my sweaty balls.
Well, I had not seen this movie before.
Ever?
Wow.

No. So I have not had a chance to make up my mind on whether this is or isn't a Christmas movie. I straddle the fence, so I look forward to some good dialogue, and especially hearing Anthony's well-thought-out reasoning.
The new trolling game.

The new way to troll Anthony is to make him paranoid by being overly nice to Anthony. So I'm looking forward to that, and I'll make my decision there. I will say, on an initial run, I agree with Anthony.

Die Hard more than Lethal Weapon just as a movie and I feel like a lot of it has to do with the aging of the film. Aside from not having cell phones, I look at, you know, Nakatagi building. I look at the cast. I look at the clothing.
I look at the way that they engage the language. It feels more timeless. Everything about this one feels very 80s, including that gorgeous feathered near mullet hair that Mel Gibson rocks.
Pretty great, right?
It is. I wish I could pull that off right now. Y'all, if I could have made that happen for tonight, I would have done it in a heartbeat. I should tease mine up a little bit.

So this movie is smart, because it took into account all the '80s teenage boys who were taking their girls on dates, when the girls were probably scoffing and rolling their eyes. Within the first two minutes of the film, a woman has her boobs out.
Boobies in the first two minutes.
But two minutes after that, you see Mel Gibson's booty, so the girls in the audience got a little something. And then after that, Danny Glover's…

Lord have mercy. That was such an uncomfortable scene. I remember that scene when I was a kid, because they showed it on TV, since they don't show anything. But if you put yourself in the scene… there are not enough bubbles. Friends reference. There are not enough bubbles in that tub. Who thought that was a good idea? They needed more bubbles. Like, a lot.
Thom, did they, though?
Or it could have been a towel or a washcloth floating around or something.
Right. Thom and Todd, you're both fathers. How do you feel? Have you had your kids walk in with
"Happy Birthday" while you're sitting in the bathtub?
For one, when you're turning 50, why are you still taking a bath?
There's a really good reason for that, and it's because baths are awesome. I did not discover baths until I was like 36, and I am a big fan.
I am too. Baths are amazing.
Just logistically speaking, they didn't want to have Danny Glover in the shower, because then they would have nothing to cover him up with.
But they came in with the birthday cake. He could have been in bed.
Yes, exactly. Sleeping in, or in his office or home office or something.

Christine makes that mistake. When she goes to the restroom, she doesn't lock doors, and Ellie comes in. When I take a bath, the door is always locked. It just makes sense: if you have children, the door is locked. You need some level of privacy. I don't know where she learned the word, but now Ellie tells her daddy, "I need you to wipe my butthole," which is really just… that's not what we call it. Though you may have that level of intimacy with your child, your child does not need to have that level of intimacy with you. There are barriers that you need to have.
That's funny, because they don't understand what they're saying.
Well, now she does, because of the reaction. But when she first said it, I don't know where she heard it. She had no idea it was a bad term.
Well, it's not like his kids are all little either. I mean, he's got the high school age daughter.
You would think she would be mortified to walk in on her dad. Yeah, and she was all just like, happy birthday, daddy. Let's chat. I mean, I don't, oh, that scene, who?
